01 · The idea

The prompt is not the secret.

Everyone can type a line into an AI. The reel argues that what makes the result look good is the four steps that happen after the line: a script built around a fast hook, a real voice timed word by word, scenes animated in code on those words, and a review of the frames before export.

The structure follows that argument. The hook shows the finished reel building itself from one line, the middle opens the four steps one by one with a tracker card that ticks as it goes, and the frame floods from warm paper to dark navy the moment the solution starts. Catalina, the Lab's character, presents it from the corner.

02 · References

What Claude needed before the first prompt.

This is the Lab's own piece, so the brand is ours and the content is the process itself. These are the style ideas it leans on, described in general terms.

Editorial paper explainer

The classic social explainer look: a warm paper background, a bold grotesque headline that types word by word, one italic serif accent word, and small mono labels at the top that count what is happening ("words timed 26", "off by 0 ms").

Problem → solution palette

A common explainer device: warm and light while the problem is on screen, dark and saturated once the answer starts. Here the switch happens on "The first one", so the viewer feels the turn before reading it.

Word-cued kinetic motion

Every stressed word changes something on stage: a prop drops, a stamp slams, a counter rolls. Between words, something keeps moving (a caret, a waveform, a playhead), so there is no frozen frame.

A progress device

A small "4 steps" tracker card in the corner turns a list into a story: each step lights up when it is named and turns green when it is done, and all four glow on the payoff.

Palette

The Lab's colours carry the frame. Props inside the scenes get their own loud colours so each machine reads at a glance.

#F6F0E6 cream#D97757 clay#141A2E navy
Presenter

Catalina, the Lab's character, from her real images: two short image-to-video clips for the opening and the close, and full-body poses from her character sheet for everything in between.

03 · One-time setup

Before the prompt.

Step 01

Install Claude Code.

Follow the official guide at docs.claude.com (Claude Code overview) for your system, then open it inside an empty project folder.

Step 02

Node 22+ and FFmpeg.

The scenes are plain JavaScript drawing on an HTML canvas. Node runs a headless browser that renders each frame, and FFmpeg turns the frames and the audio into the final MP4.

Step 03

Python 3.10+.

For the audio side: checking loudness, mixing the voice with the sound effects and reading the narration back with Whisper to confirm every word.

Step 04

An ElevenLabs API key.

Put it in a .env file in the project and ask Claude to request word-level timestamps with the audio. Those timestamps are what every animation cue reads.

Optional

A style guide for Claude.

A short Markdown file with your palette, fonts, pacing and safe zone, which Claude reads before writing any scene. We used a paid motion-design guide; your own notes work too.

04 · Claude session

One line, then the checks.

The reel started from a single typed line: make a reel about motion graphics. Below is that line written out as a full master prompt you can paste, followed by the two quality-control messages: the stills review and the final render.

00:01 · master prompt · claude code
Make a 38-second vertical edu reel for The AI Editing Lab, 1080x1920 at 30 fps, all in English. Topic: how one typed line becomes a finished motion graphics reel.

1. Script first. The hook has to land in under 2 seconds: "I made this whole animated reel by typing one line into Claude." Then open a loop ("the part that makes it look good isn't the prompt"), name the problem (most AI reels look like slop because they skip four steps), walk through the four steps one by one (script, voice, code, review), give a payoff line and close with: "Comment MOTION and I'll send you the setup." Short sentences, one idea per line.

2. Voice. Generate the narration with ElevenLabs, voice "Jessica", at natural speed (1.0, no speed-up). Get the start and end time of every word and save them to words.json. Every animation cue reads its time from a word, never from a guessed second.

3. Storyboard before code. For each of the 10 beats write what stays on stage, what changes on each stressed word, and what keeps moving between words. Invent one prop per idea: a command bar that types the line, a reel frame that plays, a wall of generic AI tiles that melts, a script page with a fishhook and a stopwatch, a mic with word pins on a waveform, a code editor above a timeline lane, a film strip under a loupe. A 4-step tracker card in the bottom-left ticks one step per section.

4. Look. Animate every scene in code on an HTML canvas, in a classic editorial paper style: warm cream #F6F0E6, clay #D97757 as the accent, a bold grotesque with italic serif accent words, small mono labels at the top. When the solution starts ("The first one"), flood the frame into dark navy #141A2E and keep it dark until the CTA, which returns to paper.

5. Layout. Keep every text and prop inside x 90-960 and y 250-1480. Leave the bottom-right corner (x 600-1080, y 1240-1920) empty: our presenter goes there later.

6. Build. Split the beats into five scene files, one per pair of beats, and build them in parallel. Sound effects only on real events (a thud on each step badge, keys while code types, an impact on the word "word"), the voice always on top, mixed to -14 LUFS with a true peak at or below -1.5 dB.

7. Process. Show me a stills sheet before the final render and wait for my approval.

What came back: a script with the hook at 0:00, a 10-beat storyboard with every stressed word mapped to a change on screen, the ElevenLabs narration with 111 time-stamped words, and five scene files built in parallel (one per pair of beats) that all read the same word clock.

00:02 · stills before render · claude code
Before the final render, export a stills sheet: one frame every 1.5 seconds starting at frame 0, with a red outline for the safe zone (x 90-960, y 250-1480). Then check every beat for two things. Motion density: does something visibly change at least once a second and on every stressed word, or is there a frozen stretch? Original work: is every prop drawn for this script, or is anything a generic placeholder? List every flat moment, every prop too small to read on a phone and every low-contrast spot, fix them all in one pass and show me the sheet again.

What came back: the first version read sparse and low-contrast on a phone: props were small and everything sat on the same paper. The fix was a second pass with bigger props filling the hero zone from the first word, and the navy palette switch for the four steps.

00:03 · final render · claude code
Approved. Now composite our presenter Catalina on top from her real images: her two short image-to-video clips at the start and at the end, and full-body poses from her character sheet in between. Each pose swaps in place with a short crossfade on a beat change; she never slides in or out. Render 1080x1920 at 30 fps, encode H.264 at 14 Mbps CBR with the mix at -14 LUFS, and give me a stills strip of the final.

What came back: 37.9 seconds at 1080×1920 and 30 fps, H.264 at 14 Mbps, the voice mixed to −14 LUFS.

05 · What Claude built

Four machines on one word clock.

SCRIPT

A hook in 1.8 seconds

A script page drops, a fishhook catches line 1 and lands it on a mini timeline at 0:00, and a stopwatch stops at 1.8 s under a 2-second limit mark.

VOICE

Word pins on the wave

A studio mic streams a waveform across a track card, and a pin with its word drops onto the wave for every word, ending on a "words timed" counter.

MOTION

0 ms off

A code editor types the scene, a timeline lane runs on the real voice clock, and the block slams onto the floor in the exact frame the playhead hits the "word" marker.

REVIEW

FLAT, then PASS

An export bar freezes at 99 %, a loupe scans a film strip, a FLAT stamp lands on an empty frame, the frame refills with motion, the stamp is ripped off and PASS slams.

key code · common.js · the palette switch
// palette switch: warm paper = the problem, dark navy = the solution
const MG_NIGHT = '#141A2E';
const MG_CREAM = '#F6F0E6';
const mgDark  = t => paletteOn(t, CUT_S1, CUT_CTA);            // 0 → 1 from step 1 to the CTA
const mgInk   = t => (mgDark(t) > 0.5 ? MG_CREAM : C.ink);     // text flips with the background
const mgFlood = (T, K, t) => paletteFlood(T, K, t, CUT_S1, CUT_CTA,
                                          { col: MG_NIGHT, x: 150, y: 500 });  // flood starts top-left
key code · common.js · the tracker reads the voice
// the 4-step tracker runs on the voice: wi(n) = start time of word n
const MG_TR = {
  born: wi(40) + 0.05,                                  // "steps."
  act:  [wi(42), wi(56), wi(66), wi(81)],               // "first", "second", "third", "last"
  done: [wi(54) + 0.15, wi(64) + 0.1, wi(78) + 0.05, wi(95) + 0.05],
  names: ['script', 'voice', 'motion', 'review'],
};
key code · step_code.js · the slam on the word
// step 3: every cue is a word, not a second
const T_THIRD = wi(66), T_THINGS = wi(73), T_MOVE = wi(74),
      T_EXACT = wi(75), T_WORD = wi(78) + 0.02;
// the timeline lane runs on the REAL voice clock, so the playhead
// reaches the marker exactly when she says "word"
const TL0 = wi(72) - 0.2, TL1 = T_WORD + 0.62;
const tlX = tt => lerp(LX0, LX1, clamp((tt - TL0) / (TL1 - TL0)));
const markX = tlX(T_WORD);

cue(T_THIRD, 'thud', -4);
cue(T_THINGS, 'swoosh', -8);
cue(T_EXACT, 'riser', -9);
cue(T_WORD, 'impact', -1);          // the block slams in the same frame
kick(T_WORD + 0.02, 1, 1);          // camera kick on the word
LEVEL UP

Five builders at once

The 10 beats were split into five scene files, one per pair of beats, and five Claude agents built them in parallel. It works because they share one layout rule, one palette and one word clock, so the pieces join without seams.

07 · Decisions

Where the taste is.

01

Show the payoff first

The hook doesn't promise a reel, it builds one: the line types, the frame fills and plays inside the first seconds.

02

Every cue is a word

No animation is placed on a guessed second. Each one reads the time of a word, so things land exactly on what you hear.

03

The palette tells the story

Paper for the problem, navy for the solution, paper again for the CTA. The turn is felt before it's read.

04

A tracker, not a list

Four steps on screen at once would be a slide. A small card that ticks one by one keeps the viewer counting to four.

05

A corner for the presenter

The bottom-right is kept empty in every scene, so Catalina never covers a prop and the props never cover her.

06

A natural voice

The narration stays at natural speed. The pace comes from the cuts and the cues, not from a faster voice.

08 · Watch out

What went wrong, and the fix.

A sped-up voice sounds rushed

An early take had the voice sped up, and it sounded hurried and less human. Back to natural speed (1.0): the reel runs a few seconds longer and every word lands.

Too sparse, too low-contrast

The first version had small props on one paper background, and on a phone it read as empty. The fix: bigger props that fill the hero zone from the first word, and the switch to dark navy when the steps start.

A presenter who slides steals the show

Catalina sliding in and out every few seconds pulled the eye away from the scenes. Now she stays in her corner and swaps poses in place with a short crossfade.

Faces alone look off

Generated face-only stickers of the character didn't feel like her. Full-body poses cut from her real character sheet did.

Read the voice back

Run the narration through Whisper before animating. If a word is misheard or the timestamps drift, every cue tied to that word lands wrong.

09 · Ship it

From render to post.

The render is not the finish line. These steps decide how the reel looks once Instagram compresses it.

Step 01

Export at a real bitrate.

Thin mono labels, waveforms and code text smear when compressed. Encode at 14 Mbps CBR.

Step 02

Check the loudness.

Aim for −14 LUFS with a true peak at or below −1.5 dB, and keep the voice above the sound effects.

Step 03

Make the cover.

The profile grid crops covers to 3:4, so keep the title and the main image between y 240 and 1680 (safer: 300 to 1480).

Step 04

Caption with the credits.

Say what was made and how, give the comment keyword, and credit the voice. On ElevenLabs' free plan, credit it as "Voice: ElevenLabs".

export · ffmpeg
ffmpeg -i render.mp4 -i mix.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v libx264 -b:v 14M -minrate 14M -maxrate 14M -bufsize 14M -x264-params nal-hrd=cbr -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -b:a 320k -movflags +faststart final.mp4
check loudness · ffmpeg
ffmpeg -i final.mp4 -af ebur128=peak=true -f null -
caption · instagram
